conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: CountertrendScalpPercentTarget
candidates.quote: When trading counter to a strong trend, the goal should be a scalp of 1 or 2 percent, since most countertrend trades just result in pullbacks that become with-trend entries.
candidates.description: For a countertrend position (against a strong prevailing trend), take profit once open profit reaches a small percentage of the entry price (1-2%), rather than a fixed dollar or point target, since countertrend trades usually only produce a brief pullback.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (a limit/profit-taking exit near a small percentage move)

complexity.reason: a single percentage comparison against the entry price

notes: rules/CATALOG.md's TakeProfit is a fixed-dollar target; this is a percent-of-entry-price target, which behaves differently across instruments and price levels and is meant for daily/weekly/monthly charts where a fixed-dollar target does not scale.

This chapter is another worked-examples chapter (charts of the DJIA 1932-33, AAPL, SPY weekly, monthly gold, monthly dollar index, AAPL round-number stalls, wheat, DNDN) narrated with the same recurring vocabulary already mined elsewhere in this book: two-bar reversals, wedges/three pushes, trend-channel-line overshoots, always-in flips, moving-average gap bars, double top/bottom flags, low2/high2 and breakout-pullback counting, measured-move targets, head-and-shoulders patterns, and trading-range uncertainty. None of those are redefined here; only the chapter's new, generalizable statements are recorded below.

candidates.name: GapPullbackFailureEntry
candidates.quote: If you can watch the stock and there is a gap opening, watch for a gap pullback and then enter on the failed pullback into the gap, as the market resumes its move away from yesterday's range.
candidates.description: When a daily buy (or sell) setup is in force and the market gaps open beyond yesterday's range in the setup's favor, do not chase the open; instead wait for an early pullback that retraces partway back into the gap, then enter once that pullback fails (a reversal bar forms and price resumes moving away from yesterday's range).
candidates.pseudocode: dailySetupLong && gapUp(open[0], priorDayHigh) && retracedIntoGap(low, gapFillFraction, priorDayHigh, open[0]) && close[0] > open[0] && close[0] > high[1]
candidates.book_order_type: enter at one tick above the failed-pullback reversal bar's high, protective stop below that bar's low (mechanized here as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open)

complexity.reason: needs a higher-timeframe (daily) setup flag, a stored prior day's high/low, a gap detector, and a reversal-bar test applied to the retracement leg -- several cross-bar and cross-timeframe pieces chained together

notes: The book gives no numeric depth for how far the pullback must travel into the gap before it counts as 'failing'; gapFillFraction is an invented parameter.

Related to reference/brooks/mined/reversals/20_gap_openings_reversals_and_continuations.json's GapOpeningDefinition and TradeWithGapDirectionBias; this candidate adds the specific wait-for-pullback-then-failure entry timing on top of those, so the dedup pass should decide whether to compose rather than duplicate.

The book also notes 'if the entry fails and your stop is hit, look elsewhere or give it only one more try if there is a second buy setup' -- an attempt-counting rule already covered by the H1/H2 family (00_front_matter.json High1Leg/High2Leg) and not re-recorded here.

candidates.name: RoundNumberMagnetOvershootTarget
candidates.quote: It will typically go 5 to 10 percent above the magnet before it pulls back, and it usually pulls back below the round number at least once before it decides what it will do next.
candidates.description: Round price levels (e.g., 100, 300, or other instrument-scale-appropriate round numbers) act as price magnets: a strong trend approaching one tends to overshoot it by roughly 5-10% before pulling back to retest the round number from above (or below, for a decline toward a round number). Usable as a profit-taking target on approach and as a pullback-entry zone on the retest.
candidates.pseudocode: roundLevel = roundToNearest(close[0], roundStep); overshootTarget = roundLevel * (1 + overshootPct); retestZone = roundLevel
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (a target/zone concept, not a specific order)

complexity.reason: which round number counts as a meaningful magnet is scale-dependent (a $93 stock vs. a $1.30 currency pair) and is a design decision before this could be coded, not just a computation

notes: Two book examples at very different price scales: FCX at 93 targeting the 100 magnet, and AAPL stalling just below 300; roundStep and overshootPct would need to be chosen per instrument.

candidates.name: BarsNearTrendLinePredictsImminentBreak
candidates.quote: Whenever five to 10 bars are close to a trend line, the odds are good that the market will soon fall below the trend line.
candidates.description: When five to ten consecutive bars have traded close to (hugging) a trend line without a clean, growing separation from it, the odds favor an imminent break through that trend line -- a precursor filter for anticipating a trend-line-break setup rather than trusting the trend line's continued support.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (a context filter that raises confidence in an upcoming trend-line-break setup)

complexity.reason: requires trend-line projection from swing pivots plus a rolling count of bars within a proximity tolerance of the projected line -- distinct from simply detecting the break itself

notes: Distinct from the already-mined TrendLineBreak family (01_example_of_how_to_trade_a_reversal.json, 03_major_trend_reversal.json), which tests the break itself; this is a predictive precursor test on approach duration.

candidates.name: BodyOnlyInsideBarVariant
candidates.quote: There, the market went sideways in a variation of an iii pattern (bodies only).
candidates.description: A variant of the inside-bar / iii setup judged only by the bar bodies (the open-to-close range) rather than the full high-low range: a bar whose body nests inside the prior bar's body even though its wick(s) may extend beyond the prior bar's high or low.
candidates.pseudocode: max(open[0], close[0]) <= max(open[1], close[1]) && min(open[0], close[0]) >= min(open[1], close[1])

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic comparing body extremes across two bars, the same shape as a full-range inside bar but restricted to open/close

notes: Compare against reference/brooks/mined/reversals/00_front_matter.json's InsideBarInclusive and TripleInsideBars, which likely use the full high/low range rather than bodies only -- the dedup pass should decide whether this is a genuinely separate primitive or a parameterization of those.

candidates.name: MinimumDailyVolumeForDayTradingEligibility
candidates.quote: If the stock is not one that you normally trade intraday but its volume is about five million shares or more, it is worth considering adding it to your basket of day trading stocks for a day or two.
candidates.description: Only consider a stock eligible for intraday trading if its recent daily volume is at least a minimum share count.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (a pre-trade eligibility filter, evaluated on the daily bar)
notes: rules/CATALOG.md's volume rules (VolumeBelowAverage, VolumeAboveAverageMultiple) test volume relative to its own recent average; this is an absolute share-count floor, a different and simpler test.

chapter_summary: Chapter 22 applies the book's pattern vocabulary to daily, weekly, and monthly charts (1932-33 DJIA, AAPL, weekly SPY, monthly gold, monthly dollar index, round-number stalls, wheat, and a news-driven stock) and discusses why longer-timeframe trading differs from 5-minute day trading (larger signal bars needing smaller size, overnight/gap risk, high-beta and news-driven stocks to avoid, broker short-sale availability). Almost all of the pattern vocabulary reuses primitives already mined elsewhere in this book. New, generalizable material captured here: a percent-of-price countertrend scalp target, a gap-then-failed-pullback entry, round-number magnet overshoot/retest levels, a bars-near-a-trend-line precursor to an imminent break, a bodies-only inside-bar variant, and a minimum daily-volume eligibility filter for adding a stock to an intraday list. Money-management, broker-constraint, fundamental-data, and news-driven statements were rejected as out of scope for a bar-based engine.
